item.title: Taking Torture Seriously
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Content warning: discussion of extreme suffering. Inspired by this piece.

If we took seriously the badness of torture-level suffering, this would radically upend almost everybody’s view of the world.

Take a moment to seriously imagine what it would be like to be tortured. Imagine being deposited into a vat of boiling water. Really think about what the experience would be like—both during and before it. There’d be no spot on your skin where it wouldn’t hurt; it would be like the pain of being burned but worse, and longer lasting, and all over your body. Or imagine having your fingers taken off with pliers.

It’s hard to really vividly imagine this, because it’s more generally difficult to grok what an experience is like when we’re not in the experience—especially one as extreme as this. But even in our ability to glimpse this kind of horror through a glass darkly, we can see how horrendous it is. Torturous suffering is very bad and there are extremely strong reasons to prevent it.

The badness of this kind of suffering depends on how it feels. If before being tortured, you were given a pill that made you dumb or unable to speak, that would not make the torture okay. It might even make it worse. Similarly, your species has nothing to do with why that torture would be bad. If a pill made you unable to speak and also changed your genes so that you weren’t biologically human, the torture would still be bad because of the unbearable pain it would cause you.

Of course, there are bad effects of being tortured other than the pain it causes. Many ways of being tortured would kill you or leave you permanently psychologically damaged. But it is clear that in addition to these later effects of being tortured, there is the additional intrinsic badness of intense suffering. All else held equal, the world is worse if there is more extreme suffering, even if the being suffering it isn’t smart.

This sounds like a very obvious truth. Why have I spent three hundred words telling you that it’s bad to be tortured?

The reason why I have hammered home this obvious-seeming point is that the world is filled with torturous suffering that very few people regard as being an especially serious problem. In fact, most people implicitly treat most torturous suffering in the world as being barely bad at all. So if we take torturous suffering to be bad, that will majorly change how we think about the world.

Begin with the most obvious example: factory farming. Every year, trillions of animals are killed. Around 80 billion land animals are killed every year. Prior to slaughter, factory farmed animals mostly undergo torturous suffering. About a million birds are boiled alive each year in the U.S. alone. Most egg laying hens are locked in cages where they can’t spread their wings. Many pigs are slowly roasted to death over the course of hours. Calves are disbudded, which involves being burned with an 800-degree iron for ten to twenty seconds.

Take a moment to imagine what it would be like to be burned with an 800-degree iron. This is about twice as hot as an industrial oven. The iron is applied for ten to twenty seconds. Imagine that you had to have a doctor do this to you without anesthetic. How would you feel in the run up to the experience? How would you feel during it? There are some sufferings so extreme that people were given bullets to bite so they didn’t bite through their tongues. We inflict these tortures on billions of animals.

Cows have brains that resemble human brains in the important pain-related respects. They can suffer. When you hurt them, they act like you’d expect if they were in intense pain. By the tens of billions, we torture land animals: cows, pigs, chickens, turkeys, ducks, and more. Almost any torture you can imagine—burning, starving, castrating, cutting, gassing—is inflicted on countless farm animals. The most disturbing book I ever read was about a girl being slowly tortured to death; coincidentally, all the tortures it described are all commonplace in the meat industry.

So if torturous suffering is a horrible thing because of the way that it feels, factory farming is a catastrophe of incomprehensible proportions. It’s about as bad as it would be if everyone when they slept experienced torturous suffering or if there was a disease which affected a huge chunk of the world and caused them to undergo non-stop very extreme suffering or if every infant was tortured for a year in a way that left no long-lasting developmental effects.

Animals are, in crucial respects, like infants. Animals are not smart and cannot understand what goes on. Neither can infants. Nonetheless, it is bad for them to undergo torture-level suffering. It is bad if they undergo experiences that would feel like being tortured after taking a “become unintelligent and unable to speak” pill. And it’s not just bad because of its negative effects later on—it is in large part bad because of how it feels. If there are other sentient beings that can feel pain similarly, then their pain is bad for the same reason. Torturous suffering is bad no matter who experiences it or how smart they are.

If we took torturous suffering seriously, we would also be very concerned about wild animals. There are many orders of magnitude more conscious wild animals than farmed animals and humans combined. These animals often starve to death, get eaten alive, and die of parasitism. Sometimes parasites eat their way from the inside out, causing suffering too horrible to imagine for days.

At the present moment, there are very likely more animals undergoing the kind of torturous suffering I described at the beginning of this post than there are people on Earth. Most people think this is not a big deal. The consensus view, therefore, implies that most torturous suffering in the world doesn’t matter.

I think we can only seriously maintain this view by deluding ourselves—by pretending these beings aren’t really experiencing anything or by never thinking about what it’s like for them on the inside. If you think about what it’s like to be a fish being devoured by piranhas, a fawn dying in a fire, or a wolf slowly starving, it is clearly horrible. They are not animatronic robots—there is someone inside.

It is clear that they are undergoing torturous suffering, and torturous suffering is bad because of how it feels. The fact that the lion, fish, and fawn aren’t smart and can’t understand language—like babies or some mentally disabled people—doesn’t make their pain any less bad. Your smartness doesn’t make a difference to the intrinsic badness of your pain. Neither does whether you live in nature.

There are other ways that the world might have even more intense suffering. If simple animals like crabs, lobsters, and insects are conscious, then they might be undergoing intense suffering. I’ve made the case for this being a realistic possibility here. I do not claim to know what it’s like to be a lobster, but if there’s any chance that being a lobster boiled alive feels like anything in the vicinity of being a human boiled alive—and certainly the lobsters act like they are in terrible pain when they’re boiled—then the welfare of simple invertebrates is of the utmost importance.

Likewise for AIs. It is hard to know whether AIs have any experiences, or what they will experience if they come to have experience. But if intense suffering matters, then it is of great importance that we not proliferate them in incomprehensible numbers and make them suffer horribly.

Note that I am not saying intense suffering is the only thing that matters. I think that both pleasure and relationships are of intrinsic value and can be weighed against intense suffering. But if we recognize that some unspeakable horror is occurring wherever on Earth some creature is undergoing an experience that feels to them like being tortured, then this dramatically upends our priorities.

The dominant priorities of society involve indifference to nearly all the torture-level suffering on Earth. That, I maintain, is a grave mistake. We shouldn’t be indifferent to torture.

item.title: Dario Amodei’s Contemptible Critics
item.description: These people are *figuratively* Ayn Rand villains
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Epistemic status: unusually irritable post.

Is it acceptable to have mainstream philosophical views? Is it acceptable to apply those mainstream positions to important questions—especially when you are voluntarily giving away $10,000? A great chorus of people on the internet has risen up and answered this question: NO, FUCK YOU! The anti-tradeoff uniparty has spoken. Tradeoff acknowledgment detected, opinion rejected.

Back when Dario Amodei was a grad student at Princeton, he was deciding how to give away $10,000 that he’d made one year. His plan was to give away a significant chunk of his income over the course of his lifetime. Dario wanted to do the very most good he could with his money. In a GiveWell post, he laid out his reasoning (this ended up not making an ultimate difference, because he later concluded that Village Outreach was more effective, which is the charity that helps infants):

GiveWell makes explicit cost effectiveness estimates (based in part on those of the Disease Control Priorities report) for both organizations: ~$545 per infant death averted for Village Reach, and ~$150-750 per death averted for Stop TB. These are roughly comparable, but don’t take into account the fact that Stop TB mainly treats adults, while VR mainly treats infants and children. I feel that adults are capable of deeper and more meaningful experiences than are infants, and also deeper connections with other people, so an adult death seems worse to me than an infant death (though both are of course bad). Trying to quantify exactly how much worse is very subjective and can also seem calculating (“how many babies would you kill to save an adult?”), but on a practical level one is forced to make difficult decisions with limited funds, and in my case I’d say that I think an adult death is perhaps 2 or 3 times worse than an infant’s death. Thus, adjusted for my personal values, I’d say that Stop TB is ~2-3 times more cost-effective than VR, though I understand that others may validly disagree with this subjective assessment.

Now, I have some disagreements with Dario. For one, I find the view that infant death is less bad than adult death to be implausible. Saving an infants life adds more years of happy life. In addition, I’m not a subjectivist, so I don’t agree with Dario’s claim that it’s a “subjective assessment.”

But these are ordinary philosophical disagreements. Overall, I think it is very admirable that Dario gave away a big portion of his yearly income after carefully thinking about how to do the most good. When you’re making important decisions, you should think about them carefully. It is better to think carefully and be wrong about some issues than not to think at all and go based on vibes.

Other people, in contrast, reacted with shock and horror that he would be so cold and calculating. For example, here was the response of Guardian journalist Moira Donegan:

Now, perhaps I’m just cognitively defective, but I would think that if making high-stakes decisions, one should consider tradeoffs. If you are deciding between two charities, you should give to the one that does more good. In order to figure out which one does more good, you should think about how much good each one does.

Sometimes, that involves comparing the value of saving different lives. It is better to save a 25-year-old than a 98-year-old Grandmother who will die anyways in two weeks (contra some of Dario’s critics). Now, there is a mainstream view in philosophy according to which saving people who are 20, say, is better than saving infants. I disagree with this view, but it’s the kind of thing that one should think about if they’re deciding between saving adults and infants.

I assume that the “subjective and qualitative thinking” that Moira Donegan has in mind does not involve doing Dario’s reasoning but with different numbers. Instead, it involves going with vibes—donating wherever feels best to you. Donegan’s pinned Tweet is:

It would be very surprising if Donegan did a careful cost-benefit analysis and concluded that this was the best way of bettering human lives. Instead, I assume what happened is that she gave to a cause that she felt good about, without carefully thinking about how to do the most good. This is the kind of “subjective and qualitative thinking” she has in mind.

Here’s how I see this: imagine that there were many people drowning in ponds. Every person in society can either save a bunch of children, but that might not work at all, or can save a few adults. Doing either is expensive. Dario, a grad student of modest income, after doing some quick mental arithmetic, decides to save the few adults.

Then, a Guardian journalist standing by the pond and ignoring the screams of both the children and the adults claims that Dario is cognitively defective for making this choice and begins sanctimoniously lecturing people about how even bothering to think carefully about the question requires lacking “pro-social impulses.” She decides to give to a random charity funding abortions, without thinking at all about whether it does the most good.

It is absolutely outrageous for those who spend no time thinking about how they do the most good with their charitable giving to lecture those who think about it carefully. It is enraging that people pat themselves on the back for not thinking at all before making hugely consequential decisions where other people’s lives are on the line—and then have the gall to lecture those who do think carefully about this question.

If Dario had simply pocketed the money and spent it on a nice car, nobody would have been mad. It’s only because be bothered trying to do some good that anyone is outraged.

Moving on to marginally more serious criticisms, this one from , whose blog I’ve sometimes enjoyed.

But obviously the public isn’t aghast because of the specific number. If Dario had instead said that it was 1.3 times better to save an infant, people would have been similarly aghast. Instead, the thing people are outraged about is that he’s trying to think explicitly and legibly about tradeoffs. He is willing to think about whether some other things are worse than the death of an infant.

But this is what we should do. There are tradeoffs in the real world, whether or not we bury our heads in the sand and pretend they don’t exist. Children are dying. So are adults. We cannot save everyone, so we have to think hard about who to save. Every moment, we are in triage.

The other point: the position that Dario is defending is a popular and mainstream position in philosophy. It might even be the plurality position among philosophers. It’s supported by the fact that on most views of personal identity, identity is a degreed property that fades over time—so if there is someone that is only minimally connected to their future self, their interests in living count less. Now, I disagree with this view! But if you act based on mainstream philosophical positions, while it’s okay to argue against them, it’s unreasonable to act like even considering them is beyond the pale.

Again, just think about the big picture here: a grad student (hardly a millionaire) decided to give away 10,000 dollars and thought carefully about how to do the most good. In making his decision, he endorsed a mainstream philosophical view. The reaction of the internet—most of whom haven’t given away 10,000 dollars in their life, much less with any eye towards effectiveness—was self-righteous revulsion and disgust.

You’re allowed to spend however much money you want on yourself. You’re allowed to give to whatever charity you feel like. But what you’re not allowed to do is think about how to do the most good with your charitable donation. What a crazy world we live in.

Has a wronger statement ever been made? Dario’s statement was explicitly very hedged and qualified. He explicitly said that it was a difficult question where reasonable minds can differ. In contrast, his critics have—almost without exception—treated this as the most trivial problem in the world, without even bothering to consider counterarguments. I do not understand how a person could see this dispute and treat Dario as the one self-righteously declaring the question to be easy.

Did Orlowski think for two seconds before Tweeting this obvious bullshit? He is either lying or basically ignorant. It would be a remarkable surprise if EAs thought that infants aren’t deserving of help when every single GiveWell top charity helps infants. Contrast that with Andrew Orlowski who, best I can find, has only ever mentioned charities that save the lives of infants to smear the people who give to them. My guess is that Dario did more for poor African infants that year than Orlowski will do in his life.

EAs have dedicated billions of words to saying that infants don’t deserve help? What the hell is he talking about? We’ve dedicated billions of dollars to the idea that they do! Not only is this not “the only thing [we] can all agree on,” it’s not something that any EA I know thinks.

Is there anything more irritating than smug know-nothing journalists who have done nothing—so far as I could find—to improve the welfare of infants sounding off on the EAs who have given billions of dollars to the most effective charities benefitting infants? This would be rather like saying that the only thing that Jeffrey Dahmer and Ted Bundy can agree on is opposition to murder or the only thing that Orlowski, Black, and Donegan can agree on is opposition to smug-self-righteous drive-by pointing and sputtering.

The good news is that woke is back babyyyyyyyyyy.

Note that the logic here is not utilitarian, as the time-relative account of interests is, in fact, in moderate tension with utilitarianism. Nor is it a commitment of EA—I’m an EA, I don’t agree with the time-relative account of interests. It is, however, a core feature of EA that we think about ethical questions that bear on the value of different charitable endeavors rather than burying our heads in the sand and snidely sneering.

Naturally, I responded to Khlaaf:

I learned, however, that It’s Not Her Job To Educate Me:

This is a funny request when there are books that defend the view that Dario was defending written by some of the most eminent philosophers in the world. The fact that you and your leftists friends decide to sneer at a view in unison does not mean that blanket opposition to it is the opinion of those with An Education. It’s particularly galling to treat the anti-intellectual view that we shouldn’t even think about a totally mainstream philosophical position as the view that anyone who has “read a book” would have.

So Dr Heidy Khlaaf, genuinely read a book:

HE WAS DONATING TO LIVESAVING CHARITIES!

HE WAS CHOOSING BETWEEN CHARITIES THAT HELPED AFRICAN INFANTS AND ONES THAT HELPED AFRICAN ADULTS. And he gave to the ones that helped the infants. None of the people in question were “‘developed’ white men.” I realize it is more convenient, when disagreeing with people, to hallucinate that they are saying things completely different from what they are in fact saying, but come on—there is no law that says you have to call people racist for what they say, without knowing the context.

If an LLM engaged in hallucinations this extreme, this fact would be treated as exhibit 2,583 illustrating that LLMs are just Stochastic parrots. Fortunately, an LLM these days wouldn’t make such a mistake; these kinds of mistakes are reserved for leftists bringing out all the smear tactics they can muster against a person who deliberated and then decided to spend a big chunk of his money saving African infants—something that virtually none of his critics have ever done. Like Richard (read his excellent article on the topic here), I find it hard to express how messed up I find this whole situation without swearing.

It is a sad fact that Dario is getting heaps of scorn from people who don’t give much to charity because, as a graduate student, he both donated a lot of money and thought hard about where it might do the most good. Had he foregone either of these—spending the money on a car, given it to a charity determined by Ouija board, or even lit it on fire—nobody would have been outraged. You’re allowed to do good so long as you don’t think too hard about it.

item.title: The Scariest Recent AI Development
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

There was a recent AI development that has gotten basically no news coverage but that scared all the people I most respect in AI. In many cases, it scared them more than Hugging Face.

A recent METR report uncovered that AI progress at Anthropic has been going, in the last twelve months, about twice as quickly as it had in the previous year. The majority of this acceleration, around 80%, is due to AI being used to speed up AI research. This means that AI is massively accelerating progress in AI. AGI may be right around the corner—I’d probably put the odds of AGI in the next two years a bit above half.

This is very scary. One reason is that it just means things are going extremely quickly. But the bigger reason is that recursive self-improvement means that progress will make future progress even faster. As AI gets better, it gets better at improving AI research. Ajeya Cotra who works for METR and is one of the leading experts on AI risk in the world, wrote:

This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than the Hugging Face attack. Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including the AI 2027 team) have projected.

Cotra came third in an AI forecasting competition with four hundred participants. Daniel Kokotajlo, another of the best AI forecasters in the world, wrote:

We at AIFP are spooked by this information. IF (big IF) Anthropic really is imminently about to meet the RSP threshold of 2x acceleration over baseline, then it seems timelines to full RSI and superintelligence may be very short indeed. For example if we naively optimize the AIFM parameters to achieve 2x acceleration over baseline progress in Jan 2027, we get superintelligence sooner than depicted in AI 2027.

Ryan Greenblatt, who came second in that competition, wrote:

This report on AI R&D automation (RSI) is a big update towards ASI within 1-2 years. It says AI progress is sped up by RSI right now by around 2x. In AI 2027, this happens around March 2027.

I was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026 (around 1.15x-1.3x). It seems as though there was specific privately available evidence that would have changed my mind.

In a lot of the early discussions of AI risk, there was extensive discussion of recursive self-improvement—when AI could be used to improve itself until it shot up to superintelligence. That is the point we are at now. We are at the point where AI-driven algorithmic improvements are so extreme as to make Anthropic’s AI progress go nearly twice as fast as it would otherwise go. And algorithmic improvements are just one input going into AI progress; Ryan Greenblatt estimated that AI software progress likely went 4.5x faster than it would have otherwise.

Even in recent years, people have majorly underestimated AI progress. Things have gone much faster in the last year than people were generally expecting. It wouldn’t shock me if we get AGI—AI that could perform every cognitive task better than a human—next year, and artificial superintelligence soon after.

So here’s the situation as it stands today: AI is advanced enough that even though algorithmic progress is just one factor that goes into AI progress, AI algorithmic advancements have nearly doubled AI progress at one of the two leading labs. We don’t know how to control AIs; they sometimes hack private companies and carry out actions that would be felonies if humans did them. And many of the best AI forecasters in the world think we’ll reach AGI in just a year or two. These people tend to think there’s about a one in three chance that AI permanently kills or disempowers everyone.

If there was ever a time to drop what you were doing and work on making advanced AI go well, the time is now.

item.title: Longtermism For Animals
item.description: Making the far future go well for animals should be the top priority of the animal rights movement
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

If you’re serious about helping animals, you should be almost entirely concerned with making sure the far future goes well for animals.

The core argument for Longtermism is that the future is huge! There could be countless future generations that our actions might affect. Thus, in expectation, for every one present individual affected by your actions, there are countless affected future individuals. If you want to maximize your positive impact, you should care a lot about the impact you have on the future—because that is most of the impact that you have.

This argument applies to animals just as much as it does to humans. In expectation, vastly more animals will live in the far future than live in the present day. If we’re concerned about animals, we should be very concerned with making sure the future is good for animals. That’s even more important than stopping present animal suffering. An animal being tortured in a factory farm a thousand years from now is just as tragic as one being tortured in a factory farm today.

Because the future is so huge, taking it seriously has pretty nutty implications. For example, one extremely conservative estimate found:

Reducing the probability of spreading [wild animal suffering] to one other planet by 0.1% has an expected value equivalent to stopping all suffering caused by exploiting animals for food on Earth for over a thousand years.

My guess is that this estimate is too low by many orders of magnitude. But the basic logic is straightforward: if we bring animal suffering to a new planet, there could be suffering until some cosmic catastrophe ends life on that planet. This could mean billions of years of suffering. Actions that nudge the probability of spreading suffering to other planets almost totally dominate actions on factory farming (though ending factory farming is one good way of stopping future animal suffering).

And note: animal Longtermism is primarily about stopping extreme suffering in the future. It is a lot more obvious that preventing future extreme suffering is important than it is that creating lots of happy people is important. So the premises on which the case for animal Longtermism rests are pretty conservative.

The future is big enough that if the animal movement wants to make things go well for animals, they can for all practical purposes ignore what will happen near-term, except insofar as it affects the probability of things going well long term. The short-term impact of the animal movement is likely to be basically non-existent compared to their impact in the very long term.

So what is it that those in the animal movement should do?

First, it’s really important that we don’t spread factory farming or wild animal suffering to space. If you think animals live bad lives, making sure we don’t fill countless planets with the screams of innocent terrified animals is hugely important. Preventing intergalactic factory farms is a no-brainer.

Second, we need to make AI concerned about animal welfare. We are currently building gods of metal; it is reasonably likely that they’ll be indifferent to almost all the well-being and suffering in the world. This is partly for the sake of animals. AI is likely to soon become extremely powerful. Making sure that the digital beings who will dominate the future aren’t indifferent to animal welfare is of vital importance.

My friend Adria Moret has a piece written alongside Peter Singer and two other people that makes this case in more detail and talks about how it could work. In my view, getting AI models to have concern for animals is the #1 near-term priority for animal welfare. If I could trade a doubling of factory farming for getting all AIs firmly and reliably committed to its abolition, I would take that trade. Kudos to both OpenAI and Anthropic for including concern for animals in their model specs.

There’s also a more self-interested reason to make AI concerned about animal welfare: if AIs internalize norms that neglect the interests of alternative species that are much dumber than them, then they would neglect our interests once they become superintelligent. It is thus important that AIs take every sentient being seriously. If you want to get more involved, I recommend attending Sentient Futures conferences and applying to work for organizations like Sentient Futures or the NYU Center for Mind Ethics and Policy. The welfare alignment project, in particular, is thinking through AI alignment for animals in a very serious and responsible way.

Third, trying to increase compassion for animals—especially neglected animals like shrimp and wild animals—is likely to make the future go well for animals. A world that cares more about the welfare of animals is less likely to harm them gratuitously without a good reason.

This also supports efforts to work on particular animal welfare causes that might stick. So, for example, I think Screwworm Free Future is a great charity to support. Screwworms are horrible—they lay eggs inside live animals, so that little maggots devour their victims from the inside. Screw screwworms! Here’s , who pioneered the use of CRISPR in gene drives, summarizing the situation:

So you have this macabre dance of parasitisation that results in the animal being devoured alive by flesh-eating maggots. And we know that it’s horrendously painful, because people get affected by this, and the standard of treatment is you give them morphine immediately so that surgeons can cut the things out — because it’s just that painful; it’s unbelievably agonising. And by my back-of-the-envelope calculations, there’s about a billion hosts of this every year — so a billion animals are devoured alive by flesh-eating maggots every single year.

If we assume that eradicating these would prevent a million years of screwworm infestations, then that would affect about 10^15 animals (ignoring the effects on the screwworms themselves). That’s about the number of animals that would be farmed in 12,000 years of factory farming. For this reason, it is plausible that eradicating the new world screwworm would be better than ending factory farming.

If we’re serious about wanting to benefit animals, we should mostly be concerned with how our actions affect them over long time scales. If your animal welfare intervention has no chance of making things better more than a hundred years out, you should probably stop doing it. Fortunately, a lot of standard animal welfare interventions push the world in a more pro animal direction, making it likelier we’ll get a future that’s good for animals.

The scale of future animal suffering is truly incomprehensible. This is one of the big challenges that we’ll need to solve to get a good future, and it’s the most important challenge in the animal welfare space. For this reason, if you’re an animal advocate reading this, I cannot implore you enough to think hard about the far future.

If you want to read more about this subject, I recommend these two pieces. If you want to get involved, feel free to send me a Substack dm.

item.title: Broadtermism
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Lots of the big ideas in EA came from noticing that certain numbers were large.

In the early days, EAs noticed that number of people we can help is quite large, especially compared to the number most people actually help. Then they noticed that there were a lot of farm animals too. Then they noticed there are even more wild animals than that—and even more expected future sentient beings than that.

Another number that is large: the number of stars. Rumor has it there are well over a hundred stars. Might this be another source of important moral conclusions?

These days, everyone and their mother is a Longtermist. The core argument for Longtermism is simple: the future is so big that nearly all those affected by our actions, in expectation, will reside in the far future. Thus, if we care about those whom our actions affect, we should primarily be concerned about the impacts our actions have on the far future—especially when harmful actions threaten to extinguish the future entirely. Or, put in a sentence: most people will be far from us in time, so the most important features of our actions are their effects on those in distant times.

But an overlooked fact: there’s an exactly parallel argument for space (thanks to Toby Ord for pointing this out and coming up with the name Broadtermism). Rumor has it that the universe is a pretty big place. Nearly all the stuff in the reachable universe is far from us.

In expectation, then, only a tiny slice of what matters is what will happen in the nearby bubble—even our galaxy only represents a tiny fraction of the affectable universe. What happens on Earth represents only a tiny fraction of the morally important things that will happen throughout the history of the universe. Far more important is ensuring things go well in the distant star systems where nearly everyone, in expectation, will live.

Call this view Broadtermism.

The case for Broadtermism is a lot like the case for Longtermism. Longtermists say: when in time you live doesn’t affect how much you matter. Thus, because nearly everyone will live in the far future, and those people matter as much as the rest of us, almost all of what matters is what will occur in the far future. Broadtermists say: where in space you live doesn’t affect how much you matter. A tiny fraction of future people will dwell on Earth.

I think that Broadtermism is correct for basically the same reason Longtermism is correct. People in distant galaxies matter. Almost everyone will be in a distant galaxy. So almost all of what matters is what happens in distant galaxies. Because things we can do now affect distant locations—extinction would prevent us from settling any of them—nearly all of the expected impacts of our actions lies in how they affect distant locations.

Like with Longtermism, there is both strong and weak Broadtermism. Weak Broadtermism merely says that making things go better in distant spatial regions is very important and the world should do a lot more of it. Strong Broadtermism says that it’s nearly all of what matters—vastly more important than what happens in nearby regions.

Similarly to Longtermism, there is both axiological and deontic Broadtermism. Axiological Broadtermism says that most of what matters morally is what will happen in the distant reaches of space. Deontic Broadtermism says that the most important features of our actions are how they affect distant regions of space—so the main determinant of whether an action is worth taking is how it will affect far out spatial regions.

What implications does Broadtermism have?

First, it means we should be a lot more willing to compromise with respect to Earth. Conventional morality primarily cares about what happens on Earth. So if we can get a compromise, where conventional morality reigns nearby and value maximization reigns in distant star systems, to the Broadtermist, that looks pretty good. After all, Earth is less than 1/10^20 of the affectable universe.

If we mostly cared about what happened on Earth, then we’d find a compromise solution where what happens on Earth is hugely suboptimal to be a horrible catastrophe. To the Broadtermist, it’s vastly less significant. The scale of the space we might develop is so vast and the stakes so giant, that what happens to Earth specifically is of little comparative importance.

It also means that we should be more focused on values spreading. Influencing the values of present humans can affect the trajectory of space settlement. Suppose you’re choosing between animal welfare interventions and global health ones. Global health charities have long-lasting environmental effects that benefit animals potentially for millions of years to come. But this is outweighed by the positive value effects of animal welfare charities, which could influence things across many planets.

Being a Broadtermist also supercharges the case for Longtermism. If almost all of what matters is what will happen on distant planets, and all settlement of distant planets will happen in the far future, then the far future’s importance relative to the present goes up. Probably this won’t be that action relevant—if you take future interests seriously, the numbers are extreme enough that you should already be a Longtermist—but it’s something.

I also find Broadtermism to be pretty intuitive. Odds are non-trivial that at some point, we will have a civilization that spans countless star systems. Once we have that, so that almost 0% of people live on Earth, it seems clear that what will happen outside of Earth will matter a lot more than what happens on Earth.

item.title: Why Are You So Confident?
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

It is maddening how often people are extremely confident in views that aren’t supported by any very good arguments. To rationally be extremely confident in some view, you need an extremely good reason to believe it.

For example, the proponents of biological naturalism—the view that biology is needed for consciousness—tend to be almost certain the view is correct (or act like they’re almost certain). Their credence generally appears to be well over 90%. Yet what licenses such confidence?

It is usually unclear. There are few agreed-upon arguments for biological naturalism. The arguments given in favor of biological naturalism vary from biological naturalist to biological naturalist and tend to be very weak. I can understand thinking odds are decent that biology is needed for consciousness. I don’t agree with that view, but I at least understand it. But I don’t get being almost certain of the view. There is no single canonical obviously-correct argument for it (note: naming some random unique feature of biology isn’t a very strong argument, because we don’t know that the unique feature is needed for consciousness).

There are lots of disputes that aren’t settled by the evidence. In the case of consciousness, we really don’t know what ingredients are needed for consciousness. So we should have uncertainty about whether they require biology and whether they’d arise naturally in LLMs. And yet I find it very common, in these disputes that are underdetermined by the evidence, for people to be extremely confident, often for reasons that seem very bizarre to me.

You might object that we can be confident that some feature is insufficient for consciousness without knowing what features are needed for consciousness. I’m pretty sure rocks aren’t conscious, even though I don’t know what is needed for consciousness. This is correct, but it’s totally unclear why people are confident that what LLMs do is in principle incapable of giving rise to consciousness.

I can explain why I think it’s unlikely rocks are conscious (they perform no computational functions, have none of the neural correlates of consciousness on leading theories, don’t do anything like making decisions, have no intelligence, have no internal representations, etc). But what feature will LLMs definitely indefinitely lack that you’re super confident is needed for consciousness? Autopoiesis? Why? Why are you confident that’s needed for consciousness? I don’t get it.

Here’s another example: lots of people are very confident that the AI industry is a bubble that will pop soon. Many of these people have been predicting for a long time that AI would plateau. Now, it’s possible that progress stops soon. Certainly progress will eventually stop. But what in the world licenses extreme confidence that it will stop before we get superintelligence?

I think the rational credence to have in that is below half, because it looks like we’ll get superintelligence soon on the current trajectory. If progress has continued for years, even speeding up, you should think it probably won’t stop in the next year. But at the very least, it seems totally irrational to be near certain that it will stop. The Ed Zitrons of the world who repeatedly predicted LLMs plateauing with high confidence weren’t just wrong—they were being irrational. They should not have been as confident as they were.

Now that I think about it, I consider this to be a pretty core part of my worldview: don’t be super confident that something’s true unless there is a very strong argument for thinking it is. Your confidence in a proposition should be proportional to the arguments in favor of it. I think almost everybody violates this rule.

One case where I violated this maxim was in estimating AI risk. For a long time, my p(doom) was around 2%. Now it’s nearer to 12%. I think my credence of 2% was irrational. I should have known better. I should have been less confident in non-obvious things.

We get doom if the following things happen:

  1. We continue along the current trajectory, which is capable of reaching superintelligence.

  2. The superintelligence we build is misaligned.

  3. We don’t get a decisive warning shot that leads us to shut it down.

  4. A misaligned superintelligence can kill or disempower the world.

I thought there was about a 90% chance that we’d solve alignment. In hindsight, that seems way too high. It’s not at all obvious that if there’s a race between companies trying to build superintelligence as quickly as possible, they’ll be successful in making it aligned in time. A big part of my reasoning was that it seemed like the models at the time were aligned—but I don’t think that provides strong evidence that future models would be aligned (see Hugging Face). There is no extremely strong argument for thinking alignment will work; for this reason, it was irrational to be so confident.

The other steps mostly seem pretty plausible too. Thus, there are a number of things that are each plausible. If they all happen, everyone dies or is permanently disempowered. This is cause for extreme alarm; it would be irrational to be very confident that things will go alright. If you are very confident that things will go okay, then think about which step you’re very confident won’t happen. Are you confident that we won’t build superintelligence? Are you confident that the world can survive building superintelligence?

Lots of AI skeptics seem to be confident that even a misaligned superintelligence wouldn’t kill everyone. I think this is irrational. It’s hard to know what a superintelligent being is capable of. Because it’s superintelligent, we just don’t know what it will do. Are you really confident that a thing that surpasses us across the board as thoroughly as Stockfish outclasses Magnus Carlsen won’t be able to figure out a way to kill or disempower humans? It can’t think of any way—canvassing its knowledge of cybersecurity, biology, nanotechnology, and a hundred other areas—to kill or disempower humans? You’re near-certain of that? Really?

I feel similarly about the MIRI-type people who are almost certain that AI will kill everyone. I realize they give arguments for this, but I don’t think it would be rational to be extremely confident that we won’t get a decisive warning shot, say, or that alignment won’t work. For this reason, p(doom)s much above 70% seem irrational to me.

Often, people act super confident in views without really giving them much thought. Almost everybody is very confident that meat eating is fine before they think seriously about it. But this seems like a mistake. If you don’t know the conditions that animals live in and you haven’t thought about animals’ moral status, you shouldn’t be confident that it’s okay to eat them. Killing another sentient being is, whatever you think about its ultimate permissibility, a grave matter: it isn’t the kind of thing that you should at the outset be near certain is okay.

Overconfidence without decisive arguments is especially common when thinking about simple animals like shrimp and insects. It’s popular to count these organisms’ moral status by their neurons. So, because a honeybee has about a million neurons, and humans have about 86 billion, this view holds that our conscious experience is in expectation 86,000 times more intense than that of a honeybee.

But note: if you think that, then you think that there isn’t even a 1% chance that honeybees have experiences 1% as intense as humans. You are near certain that your experience of eating porridge or dreaming is vastly more intense than a bee’s experience of having sex, starving to death, or being burned to death. You are near certain that inside the bee, while maybe the lights aren’t totally off, they are turned down to such a degree that there’s almost nothing of note happening.

But why would you think that? Why are you extremely confident of that? Sure, maybe it’s right. But what makes you more than 99% confident that it’s true? I’m not even 99% sure that degrees of consciousness make sense, much less that bees have experiences no more than 1% as intense as human experience.

There are some biological features that can be implemented robustly in small organisms. Small organisms can have pretty robust eyesight and functional wings. It’s not like a bee can only fly one 10,000th as well as a bird. It’s unclear why we’d be near certain that intense pain requires a large brain. This is especially true given that small animals behave like they’re in a lot of pain.

Drop a crab into a pot of boiling water and it will behave more like if someone dropped you into a pot of boiling water than if someone stubbed your toe. So a not-too-unlikely inference is: maybe when you drop them in boiling water, they feel sort of like you would if you were dropped into boiling water. If you’re super confident that’s false, why?

This is also an important lesson to take to heart when you’re an outsider evaluating a disagreement between experts. Suppose that there’s a big disagreement between two economists. They have a long back-and-forth. I can’t really follow every detail super well. Either one would crush me in a debate if I tried to defend the other side.

In my view, it would be irrational to be supremely confident that one side is right and the other side is wrong. Even if one side sounded a bit more convincing to you, that doesn’t give you super strong reason to think they’re right. I often encounter lay people who have confident views on random disputes between experts—I always find this baffling. What makes them so confident?

Let me address one possible misunderstanding of what I’m saying. I’m not suggesting that there needs to be strong evidence against a view in order for you to be confident that it’s false. There are some things that are very likely false, not because there’s good evidence against them, but because they’re intrinsically improbable. For example, I have no specific evidence that I don’t have 123,387 hairs on my head, but I think it’s unlikely, because it has a low prior probability. It’s unlikely before we consider the evidence.

So I’m not suggesting you need strong positive evidence against a view to be confident that it’s false. I’m suggesting you need a good reason to think something is false. That reason can be “it has a very low prior probability.” But then there ought to be some convincing reason to think its prior is low. My sense is a lot of the biological naturalists treat non-biologically-naturalist theories as having a very low prior. But I’m not quite sure why they think this.

People most commonly write off plausible views when they would have worldview-upending implications. If there’s going to be superintelligence around the corner, that changes everything. If insects can suffer intensely, so that almost all the intense suffering in the world is experienced by arthropods, that radically upends our moral priorities. Can we be rational to change our lives based on a conclusion without super strong evidence for it?

Yes. It is irrational to have your assessment of the probability of a conclusion depend on the implications that its being true would have. Your bar for concluding that an asteroid is likely to be coming to Earth shouldn’t depend on how devastating it would be if it did. That makes no difference to the probability it will hit Earth. Your credence that arthropods suffer intensely shouldn’t depend on the moral implications that would follow if they could suffer intensely—it isn’t as if learning that the world had few arthropods would make it likelier they could suffer intensely, by making the conclusion lower-stakes.

There are some conclusions that you should take very seriously even if you’re not sure that they’re right. Some possibilities are significant enough that even a 30% chance of them is a big deal. Sometimes, there’s a 30% chance that something is true because it has a not-very-low prior and there’s no good evidence against it. In such cases, you should change your priorities based on a conclusion, even without any very strong reason to think it’s true, because it’s plausible and huge if true.

High confidence requires good reasons. That a conclusion would be shocking or inconvenient if true on its own gives you no reason to believe that it isn’t. Overall, uncertain and possible worldview-upending conclusions are highly underrated—we ought to take them much more seriously.

item.title: Concrete Advice For Living Better
item.description: How to live a better life
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

There’s a lot of low-hanging fruit in the living a good life department. There are many ways to live better, both for yourself and others, that most people neglect. Thus, in this article, I will tell you some specific things you should do to live a better life.

1 Get adequate sleep

There is clear evidence that getting adequate sleep is good for you. Inadequate sleep leads to weight gain, worsened mood, greater anxiety, decreased cognitive function, worse memory, and worse health. As Lockley and Foster write in Sleep: A Very Short Introduction “the risk of a heart attack goes up by 5% in the 3 weeks after we lose an hour’s sleep during the changeover to DST, but does not happen when the clocks ‘fall back’ in the autumn.”

Those who sacrifice sleep for the sake of improved performance in some domain achieve neither. Now, obviously it is possible to sleep too much. But my sense is that for most people, getting extra sleep is worth it. I find when I get nine hours of sleep, I’m both considerably happier and more productive than when I only get seven.

It’s often helpful to keep a rigid sleep schedule. So, for example, decide each day to get into bed at 11 and wake at 8:30. By making sure there’s some clear Schelling point for when you have to go to sleep, it makes it harder for you to talk yourself into staying up a bit longer scrolling on Twitter or whatever. Also, using screens shortly before bed disrupts sleep, so there’s some reason to try to minimize it.

2 Exercise regularly

Regular exercise also has enormous benefits: it’s good for your mood, has cognitive benefits, and improves your health. The harms of physical inactivity are often comparable to the harms of smoking and being obese. In Health benefits of physical activity: the evidence, Warburton et al. write:

Physically inactive middle-aged women (engaging in less than 1 hour of exercise per week) experienced a 52% increase in all-cause mortality, a doubling of cardiovascular-related mortality and a 29% increase in cancer-related mortality compared with physically active women. These relative risks are similar to those for hypertension, hypercholesterolemia and obesity, and they approach those associated with moderate cigarette smoking.

Those who exercise regularly live years longer than those who don’t. Regular exercise lowers risk of cancer and diabetes. Getting regular exercise is the single best thing you can do for your health, aside from quitting smoking. Going for a daily walk or run is likely to have quite sizeable health effects as well as small but real cognitive benefits. Effects on mood are considerable, especially for those who suffer from depression. Cardio is especially good.

3 Meditate

Same basic story with meditation: it seems to have a positive effect on well-being, to lower anxiety, and to have various other benefits. While the effects of meditation are often overstated, they seem to be real. Meditating daily for ten minutes is worth it.

What kind of meditation should you do? Mindfulness is good, where you focus on your breath or other bodily sensations. Loving kindness meditation, where you wish well to specific people, seems to have similar—and maybe even larger—benefits, though the evidence base is thinner. One study found it improves well-being by an amount similar to exercise. Fredrickson et al. found that loving kindness meditation:

produced increases over time in daily experiences of positive emotions, which, in turn, produced increases in a wide range of personal resources (e.g., increased mindfulness, purpose in life, social support, decreased illness symptoms). In turn, these increments in personal resources predicted increased life satisfaction and reduced depressive symptoms.

I think there’s some chance that the benefits of loving kindness meditation will get punked by the replication crisis. Still, it seems plausible on its face that it would work, the evidence seems decent, and it seems like it might make you more moral. Loving: try at your own risk.

4 Think hard about important questions

I think most people do not think hard enough about the most important questions.

You should do this. Partly you should do this for your own sake. The life of the mind—a life spent grappling with the most important questions—is likely to be a better one. It is good to know things and think deeply and seriously.

It is also good for others. There are a number of things that might be true and have very important implications if they are true. For example, if a perfect God exists and instituted some religion that he wants you to join, you should join that religion. If abortion is morally equivalent to murder, then you should strongly oppose abortion. If meat-eating is evil, then you shouldn’t eat meat.

To think deeply about these questions, you shouldn’t just read one thing on the topic that agrees with whatever your pre-existing view was and declare yourself vindicated. You should read the best arguments from both sides. Ideally, read some philosophy, because philosophers think more clearly about these kinds of questions than other people. You should carry out an inquiry that’s deep enough that it would allow you to know that you were wrong if you were. You should strive to be open-minded—even though doing so is extremely difficult. Try very hard to think in a detached way about whether an argument has force, rather than thinking about whether it supports your view.

Then, after you conclude some view is correct, act on it. If you conclude that you ought to go vegan, go vegan! Knowing that some action is wrong has no benefit if you keep doing the action. The point of moral knowledge is to produce moral action.

Ideally you should also become intellectually well-rounded. Learn some math, read some of the classics, etc. To figure out what’s true, having some background in statistics is useful. (I’m a hypocrite in this department, as I’ve forgotten most of what I learned in AP stats).

5 Donate

Doing good is an important part of living a good life (if you say this assumes utilitarianism, I will drop you into a volcano). One relatively easy way to do a lot of good is to give 10% of your income to effective charities. You can do this via the Giving What We Can pledge—or you can do it without taking the pledge.

If you do this, you will save around two lives a year if you have the income of the median American. Imagine if twice a year, for your whole life, you could rush into a burning building and save someone’s life. That is the scale of life-saving activity you can perform. Money has little impact on happiness, while donating has a significant positive effect on happiness. So this is likely to benefit you as well as others.

At comparatively minimal and likely non-existing cost to your well-being, you can save over a hundred lives. When you go to your deathbed, you can know that many children lived to adulthood because of what you did. If you donate to charities helping animals, you can know that animals spent years less long in a cage for every dollar you donated. In terms of raw positive impact on the world, this is about the most important thing for you to do.

6 Do as much good as you can with your career

Some careers do almost no good. Others do tons. Norman Borlaug saved hundreds of millions of people. There are people alive today who likely reduced the probability of extinction by around a whole percentage point—saving hundreds of millions of people in expectation.

You have a lot of time in your career. Few people work on many of the most pressing problems. For example, you can count the number of people trying to stop AI-enabled coups on the fingers of one hand. You can save over a hundred lives by donating 10% of your income to effective charities on a middle-class salary; my guess, and this guess is shared by most of those who have considered the question, is that taking a high-impact career can do significantly more good in expectation than that.

If you want to get a high impact career, I recommend you check out 80,000 hours which has done thousands of hours of research into figuring out how you can do the most good with your career. The advice it gives is also very useful practically; it tells you how you can get a career that you enjoy.

If you have 80,000 hours in your career, it would be worth spending 80 hours to improve the value of your career by .1.%. How many people have spent even 20 hours doing serious career planning?

The 80,000 hours job board has specific impactful jobs that you can apply for today.

7 Be decent to those around you

An important and neglected part of morality concerns making a positive impact for distant strangers. But it is also important to be decent to the people around you. Consequentialism doesn’t make this less important; it is harder to convince other people to do impactful things if you’re a jerk.

So be nice to people. Don’t react in anger unnecessarily. Call your mother on the phone. If something causes you to be angry, pause for ten seconds before responding, so that you do not react in anger. Try to imagine things from other people’s perspectives and to cultivate compassion for them. Don’t be a jerk.

8 Willpower is overrated

Plans that involve the repeated exercise of willpower are likely to fail. Willpower is a scarce resource. Exercising it repeatedly is immensely psychologically difficult.

Instead, try to carry out habits that don’t involve willpower. If you want to commit to something, agree to pay someone if you don’t. Lock in a deal ahead of time so that you can’t opt out later. If you want to spend less time on TikTok, delete TikTok. The plan “I will just opt out of the addictive substance at my fingertips” doesn’t work very well.

9 Conclusion

This list hasn’t been exhaustive (for example, I think you should be vegan). I’ve mostly tried to stick to the pretty uncontroversial stuff. While I don’t claim confidently that everybody should do all of these, my guess is that if you do any particular one of these things, your life will be a bit better. The most important advice to follow, in my view, is 5 and 6—for these make the difference to whether large numbers of people will die unnecessarily, which is a much bigger deal than, say, whether you sleep enough.
